bipartite.note: The translation reorders the poem's logic: it opens with the oath and the speaker's naive trust (L1-L2, roughly corresponding to shimo's 'chikaiteshi hito' content moved to the front), then moves to being forgotten/scorned and the penalty of death (L3-L4, corresponding to kami's 'wasuraruru mi' content merged with shimo's death-penalty idea). The original paradoxical pivot — 'I do not grieve for myself, but for his endangered life' — is lost; instead the translation reads as a fairly linear reproach culminating in a wish/near-curse of death upon the unfaithful lover, inverting the source's selfless concern into something closer to vindictive judgment.

kigo_handling.note: The source poem itself contains no seasonal imagery (a purely emotional koi-uta), and the translation likewise contains no seasonal markers or atmosphere; this is consistent with the source's lack of kigo.

entries.content_summary: The oath he swore ('chikaiteshi') is foregrounded as the poem's opening image.
The speaker's naive belief in his constancy — an invented interpretive gloss on 'hito' (the man who swore) blended with an added notion of her having 'dreamt' he would be faithful.
'Forgotten' clearly renders 'wasuraruru' (being forgotten), but 'scorned the penalty' introduces a moralizing judgment not present in source.

The idea of death connects to 'hito no inochi no oshiku mo aru kana' (the preciousness/peril of his life), but here it is inverted into an almost vengeful wish for his death/punishment rather than tender anxiety for his life.

line_mapping.structural_note: The translation compresses and reorders the five ku into four rhymed lines, front-loading the oath and back-loading 'forgotten' and 'death,' which inverts the source's original sequence (self-abandonment first, concern for his life second) and changes the emotional valence from selfless worry to something closer to reproach or a near-curse.

Dickens.translator_strategy: Dickens prioritizes a rhymed, quatrain-form English lyric over literal fidelity, reshaping the poem's selfless paradox into a more conventional narrative of betrayal and retribution.

bipartite.note: The paradox structure is retained (I do not mind for myself, but I grieve for him), but the second half loses the specific reasoning about the sacredness of the broken vow and divine punishment for oath-breaking; it is compressed into a generic 'grieve for his life's sake', weakening the piercing irony of the original where her concern is specifically that his oath-breaking endangers his life.

kigo_handling.note: The source poem has no seasonal imagery at all (koi-uta), and this translation likewise contains no seasonal reference or imagery of any kind, consistent with the original's purely emotional/relational content.

entries.content_summary: I do not mind of myself (denial of self-pity)
but for his own life's sake

line_mapping.structural_note: The five ku are compressed into four lines; ku3 (誓ひてし, 'who vowed') is entirely dropped, so the vow itself — the crux of why his life is at risk — disappears, leaving 'his own life's sake' as a vaguer, less motivated concern.

Noguchi.translator_strategy: Noguchi prioritizes a compact, natural-sounding English paraphrase of the emotional paradox over preserving every semantic unit, sacrificing the vow (誓ひてし) and its implied divine retribution for economy and readability.

bipartite.note: The source's paradox hinges on the speaker explicitly setting aside her own suffering ('mi o ba omowazu') to redirect concern entirely onto the man's peril from broken vows. Porter's version preserves a two-part structure (self-resignation vs. concern for the man) but reverses the emotional thrust of the shimo: instead of fearing for the man's life/safety as punishment for oathbreaking, Porter has the speaker praying the gods will 'absolve' him — an almost merciful, forgiving gesture rather than an anxious, piercing reproach about mortal danger. This changes the paradox from 'my own suffering doesn't matter, but I fear for your life' into 'I don't lament my heartbreak, and I even wish you well despite your broken vow,' softening the irony into simple generosity, thus inverting the emotional logic even though the two-part shape survives.

kigo_handling.note: No seasonal imagery exists in the source poem, and none appears in this translation; it remains a purely emotional/relational poem about heartbreak and broken vows.

entries.content_summary: Declares she does not lament her broken heart, i.e. the state of being forgotten/abandoned
Adds a resigned 'I bow to destiny,' an interpretive gloss on her acceptance of fate not explicitly in the source
Shifts to the man who broke his solemn oath (誓ひてし人)
Introduces prayer to the Gods, echoing the source's concern with divine consequence for oathbreaking but reframed as intercession rather than fear
Completes the prayer: wishes the gods 'absolve' him from his vow, replacing the source's anxious concern for his life ('命の惜しくもあるかな') with a wish for forgiveness/release

line_mapping.structural_note: Porter compresses the kami's three ku into two lines and expands the shimo into three lines, using rhyme (heart/bow, oaths/now/vow) to unify the stanza; the emotional content of the shimo is substantially altered from fear-for-his-life to a plea for divine forgiveness, softening the original's ironic reproach into a gentler, more magnanimous sentiment.

Porter.translator_strategy: Porter prioritizes a rhymed, hymn-like English quatrain-plus-couplet form over precise semantic fidelity, substituting the original's anxious foreboding about the man's fate with a softer, more forgiving prayer for his absolution.

bipartite.note: The translator preserves the paradoxical turn: lines 1-2 assert the speaker's indifference to her own forgotten state, while lines 3-5 shift concern entirely to the man's peril for having broken his vow, mirroring the source's redirection of sympathy from self to the faithless lover.

kigo_handling.note: The source poem itself contains no seasonal imagery (it is a koi-uta about broken vows), and the translation likewise contains no natural or seasonal imagery of any kind, consistent with the source's lack of a kigo.

entries.content_summary: Though forgotten now — renders 忘らるる (being forgotten)
For myself I do not care — renders 身をば思はず (I do not think of myself)
He, by oath, was pledged — renders 誓ひてし (he who swore)
And his life, who is forsworn — renders 人の命の, adding 'forsworn' to emphasize the broken vow
That is, ah! so pitiful — renders 惜しくもあるかな, the exclamation of pity/regret for his life

line_mapping.structural_note: The translation maps almost one-to-one onto the five ku, preserving the original five-line structure and sequential logic without compression or inversion; the only minor expansion is the insertion of 'forsworn' in line 4 to make explicit the broken-vow theme already implicit in the source.

McCauley.translator_strategy: McCauley pursues a close, line-by-line literal rendering that mirrors the five-ku structure and preserves the poem's paradoxical shift from self-neglect to concern for the faithless man's fate, at the cost of natural English syntax and idiom.
